tagline: The first half of a two-volume history: the story of Jesus, Savior of the poor, the outsider, and the lost, told to a man named Theophilus so that he might know the certainty of what he had been taught.
overview:
Luke is the longest of the four Gospels and the first of two books by the same author; the second is the Acts of the Apostles. It opens with something none of the other Gospels has, a formal preface in polished Greek that explains the author's method: many have written accounts, the material was handed down by eyewitnesses, and he has investigated everything carefully in order to write an orderly account for “most excellent Theophilus” (1:3). Then the story begins in the temple in Jerusalem, with an old priest and a promise, and moves through the births of John the Baptist and Jesus, Jesus' ministry in Galilee, a long section on the road to Jerusalem, and his death, resurrection, and ascension.

Much of Luke's material appears in no other Gospel. Only Luke tells of the shepherds at the manger, the boy Jesus in the temple, the Good Samaritan, the lost coin and the lost son, the rich man and Lazarus, Zacchaeus in the tree, the thief on the cross who is promised paradise, and the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. These stories share a direction. The good news comes to the poor, the sick, women, Samaritans, tax collectors, and sinners, and it comes with joy. Jesus sums up his own mission near the end: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10).

Luke matters because it shows the story of Jesus as history that fulfills Israel's Scriptures and opens toward the whole world. It begins among faithful Jews waiting in the temple for the consolation of Israel and ends with the risen Jesus explaining that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled (24:44), and that repentance and forgiveness will be preached to all nations. Acts then tells how that happened. Between them the two volumes make up more than a quarter of the New Testament, more than any other single author contributed.
author:
The Gospel does not name its author, but the tradition that Luke wrote it is early and uniform, and no other name was ever attached to it. Irenaeus of Lyon (Against Heresies 3.1.1, around AD 180) says Luke, the follower of Paul, set down in a book the gospel Paul preached, and in 3.14.1 he argues from the we passages of Acts that Luke was Paul's inseparable companion. The Muratorian fragment, a Latin list of accepted books, calls the third Gospel the work of Luke the physician, whom Paul took with him, and adds that Luke did not see the Lord in the flesh. It is usually dated to the late second century, though Albert Sundberg (1973) and Geoffrey Hahneman (1992) argued for the fourth. A Latin prologue to Luke, one of the so-called anti-Marcionite prologues, of disputed date, calls him a Syrian of Antioch and a physician who died unmarried at eighty-four in Boeotia.

Paul names Luke three times: “Luke, the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), a fellow worker (Philemon 24), and “Only Luke is with me.” (2 Timothy 4:11). Colossians 4:10-11 seems to list him apart from the coworkers who are Jewish, so many think Luke was a Gentile, though some dispute the inference. The strongest internal evidence is in Acts, where the narrative shifts without comment from they to we (16:10-17, 20:5-21:18, 27:1-28:16; Codex Bezae adds a we at Antioch in 11:28). The traditional reading is that the author was there. Others think he used a travel diary, his own or another's. Vernon Robbins (1978) proposed that first-person narration was a convention of ancient sea-voyage stories; Colin Hemer and Susan Marie Praeder, among others, doubted that such a convention existed. Philipp Vielhauer's essay on the Paulinism of Acts (1950) argued that the theology Acts gives Paul is too unlike his letters for a companion to have written it; defenders reply that a companion's portrait need not reproduce the letters' arguments.

The claim that medical vocabulary proves a physician wrote the book (W. K. Hobart, The Medical Language of St. Luke, 1882) was answered by Henry Cadbury (The Style and Literary Method of Luke, 1920), who showed that educated writers without medical training used the same words. The case now rests on the tradition and on Acts. Whoever he was, the author wrote the most literary Greek in the Gospels and knew the Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament) intimately.
date:
Luke was written before Acts, since Acts 1:1 refers back to it, so the two are dated together. Three positions have serious defenders.

An early date, before about AD 62, was argued by Adolf von Harnack (The Date of the Acts and of the Synoptic Gospels, 1911), John A. T. Robinson (Redating the New Testament, 1976), and Colin Hemer (1989). Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years (around AD 60 to 62) and says nothing of his death, Nero's persecution, or the fall of Jerusalem; on this view Luke stopped because events had reached his own day.

A date between about AD 75 and 90 is the majority view, held for example by Joseph Fitzmyer (about 80 to 85) and Raymond Brown. Its reasons are that Luke used Mark, usually dated to the late 60s or around 70, and that Luke's wording of Jesus' warning, “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies” (21:20), and of enemies building an embankment against the city (19:43), reads like knowledge of the Roman siege of AD 70. Defenders of the earlier date answer that the language draws on Old Testament siege oracles and that Acts may end where it does because Paul preaching unhindered in Rome is the goal of the story (28:31).

An early second-century date, around AD 110 to 125, is argued by Richard Pervo (Dating Acts, 2006) and Joseph Tyson (Marcion and Luke-Acts, 2006). Steve Mason (Josephus and the New Testament, 1992) argued that Luke-Acts shows knowledge of Josephus's Antiquities, finished in AD 93 or 94, pointing among other things to the order of Theudas and Judas in Acts 5:36-37; others find the parallels too general to prove dependence. The latest possible date is set by Marcion, who used a form of Luke by about AD 144, and by P75, a papyrus copy of Luke from around 200.
setting:
The story is set in Judea and Galilee under Roman rule, from the last years of Herod the Great (who died about 4 BC) to the governorship of Pontius Pilate (about AD 26 to 36). Luke anchors it in public history more carefully than any other Gospel writer. The birth is dated by the emperor Augustus and a census under Quirinius, governor of Syria (2:1-2), and John's preaching by the fifteenth year of Tiberius, with Pilate governing Judea, Herod Antipas ruling Galilee, and Annas and Caiaphas holding the high priesthood (3:1-2). The Jerusalem temple, rebuilt on a grand scale by Herod the Great, frames the book: it opens with Zechariah burning incense there and closes with the disciples praising God in its courts (24:53).

The first readers are harder to place. Theophilus has a Greek name meaning friend of God, and the title “most excellent” was used for men of rank, such as the governors Felix and Festus in Acts (23:26, 26:25). He may have been a patron who paid for the book's copying and circulation, a common practice for ancient authors, as Josephus dedicated his later works to one Epaphroditus, or a believer of standing who had been instructed in the faith. Beyond him the book seems written for a mainly Gentile church in a Greek-speaking city of the eastern empire, one that wanted to know how a movement born among Jews in Judea came to include people like them, and whether it could be trusted. Tradition has suggested Antioch, Achaia, and Rome; the book itself does not say.
purpose:
Luke states his purpose himself: he has written so that Theophilus may know the certainty of the things he has been taught (1:4). The book confirms faith by setting out what happened in order, grounded in eyewitness testimony. It also answers questions a Gentile church faced. Was this the continuation of Israel's faith or a new sect? Luke shows Jesus fulfilling God's promises to Israel and the inclusion of Gentiles planned from the start (2:32). Was it a threat to Roman order? Roman officials find no fault in Jesus (23:4, 23:14-15, 23:22) or, in Acts, in Paul. Who belongs? The poor, the sinful, and the outsider are welcomed, and the rich and respectable are called to repentance with everyone else.

The purpose runs across both volumes. Henry Cadbury's The Making of Luke-Acts (1927) established the habit of reading the two books as one work in two parts, and the evidence is strong: the same dedicatee, the summary of the first book at the start of the second (Acts 1:1-2), the ascension told at the end of one and the start of the other, and themes (the Spirit, prayer, witness, the nations, Jerusalem) that begin in the Gospel and are completed in Acts. Mikeal Parsons and Richard Pervo (Rethinking the Unity of Luke and Acts, 1993) accepted one author but questioned whether the books share one genre and one narrative design, and the church itself never copied them together: in the manuscripts Luke stands among the Gospels and Acts travels with the letters.
story: Luke picks up the Old Testament story where it paused. Its first chapters are full of the language of the Greek Old Testament: an old childless couple like Abraham and Sarah or Elkanah and Hannah, the angel Gabriel from Daniel, and songs that echo Hannah's prayer and the Psalms. The long silence after the prophets ends with John, who comes in the spirit and power of Elijah, as Malachi had promised. The Gospel then tells how God's promises to David and to Abraham are kept in Jesus, and it reaches further back than any other Gospel, tracing his line through David and Abraham to Adam, son of God (3:38). It ends where Acts begins, with the ascension and the command to wait in Jerusalem for power from on high. Acts carries the same story from Jerusalem to Rome, so that the two books together cover the arc from the temple in Jerusalem to the capital of the Gentile world. Hans Conzelmann (Die Mitte der Zeit, 1954; English 1960) described Luke's history as three periods, Israel up to John, the ministry of Jesus as the middle of time, and the age of the church; later scholars have questioned how sharply Luke divides them, but the book plainly sees itself as the hinge between Israel's Scriptures and the church's mission.
christ: Luke presents Jesus as Savior, a title the angels announce to shepherds (2:11) and one that Matthew and Mark never use. He is the Son of David who will reign forever, the Son of God conceived by the Holy Spirit, and the prophet anointed by the Spirit to preach good news to the poor. In his first sermon at Nazareth he reads from Isaiah 61, “The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor” (4:18), and says the Scripture is fulfilled that day. Luke calls him Lord in the narrator's own voice, the title the Greek Old Testament uses for God, far more often than Matthew or Mark do. He also stresses that the Messiah's suffering was necessary: the risen Jesus explains to the Emmaus disciples, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, what was written in all the Scriptures about himself (24:27). And Luke's Jesus is the one who seeks the lost: he eats with sinners, forgives a criminal dying beside him, and prays for those who crucify him. The church confesses on this ground that Jesus is truly God and truly man, crucified for sinners, bodily raised (Luke insists he eats fish before the disciples, 24:42-43), and ascended to the Father.
reading:
Read Luke as an ancient history written by a believer, not a modern biography. Luke selects and arranges, sometimes by theme rather than strict chronology, and he often pairs a man and a woman (Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna, the shepherd with his sheep and the woman with her coin). Watch the meals, the prayers, and the word today. The central section (9:51-19:27) is framed as the road to Jerusalem, but it gathers teaching on discipleship, wealth, prayer, and the kingdom more than it logs a route.

Readers comparing Luke with Matthew and Mark will meet the Synoptic problem: the three share much wording and order, so one must have used another or a common source. The Two-Source hypothesis, formulated by Christian Hermann Weisse (1838) and H. J. Holtzmann (1863) and refined by B. H. Streeter (The Four Gospels, 1924), holds that Matthew and Luke independently used Mark and a lost sayings source called Q (German Quelle, source); it remains the majority view. The Farrer hypothesis, from Austin Farrer's essay On Dispensing with Q (1955) and defended by Michael Goulder and Mark Goodacre (The Case Against Q, 2002), keeps Mark first but has Luke using Matthew too, making Q unnecessary. The Griesbach or Two-Gospel hypothesis, from J. J. Griesbach (1789) and revived by William Farmer (The Synoptic Problem, 1964), puts Matthew first, Luke second using Matthew, and Mark as a digest of both. Luke says only that he drew on earlier accounts and eyewitnesses (1:1-2), which fits each view.

structure.title: Preface to Theophilus
structure.summary: One long, formal sentence tells how the work was made: earlier accounts, eyewitness tradition, careful investigation, and an orderly account written so that Theophilus may know the certainty of what he was taught.

structure.title: The births of John and Jesus
structure.summary: Opening “In the time of Herod king of Judea” (1:5) and written in the style of the Greek Old Testament, paired announcements, births, and songs show God keeping his promises to Israel, ending with the boy Jesus in his Father's house.

structure.title: Preparation for ministry
structure.summary: A six-part date by emperor, governor, tetrarchs, and high priests (3:1-2) opens John's preaching. Jesus is baptized and named beloved Son, his genealogy runs back to Adam, and he is tested in the wilderness.

structure.title: Ministry in Galilee
structure.summary: Marked by “Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit” (4:14), this section opens with the sermon at Nazareth and moves through healings, forgiveness, the call of disciples, and teaching, to Peter's confession and the first predictions of suffering.

structure.title: The road to Jerusalem
structure.summary: The turning point is marked in the text: “As the day of His ascension approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem” (9:51). Reminders of the destination recur (13:22, 17:11, 18:31) as Jesus teaches on discipleship, prayer, wealth, and the kingdom, with many parables found only in Luke.

structure.title: Teaching in Jerusalem
structure.summary: Marked by “He went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem” (19:28), Jesus enters the city, weeps over it, clears the temple, answers his opponents, and foretells Jerusalem's destruction and the coming of the Son of Man.

structure.title: The passion
structure.summary: Jesus shares the Passover meal, prays on the Mount of Olives, is betrayed, tried before the council, Pilate, and Herod, crucified between two criminals, and buried.

structure.title: Resurrection and ascension
structure.summary: The women find the tomb empty, the risen Jesus meets disciples on the Emmaus road and in Jerusalem, opens the Scriptures to them, and is carried up into heaven, and the disciples return to the temple praising God.

themes.title: Good news to the poor
themes.body: Luke gives more attention to wealth and poverty than any other Gospel. Mary sings that God has filled the hungry and sent the rich away empty (1:53), Jesus' first sermon announces good news to the poor (4:18), his beatitudes bless the poor and pronounce woes on the rich (6:20-26), and parables like the rich fool and the rich man and Lazarus warn against trusting in possessions. Zacchaeus, a rich tax collector who gives away half his goods, shows what repentance can look like with money.

themes.title: Women and outsiders
themes.body: Women are prominent throughout Luke: Elizabeth, Mary, and Anna in the birth stories, the women who supported Jesus from their own means (8:1-3), Martha's sister Mary sitting at his feet as a disciple (10:38-42), and the women who witness the cross and first hear of the resurrection. Samaritans, whom many Jews despised, appear as the neighbor in the parable and the one grateful leper among ten. Tax collectors and sinners are welcomed at Jesus' table, which scandalizes his critics.

themes.title: Prayer
themes.body: Luke shows Jesus praying at the turning points of his life: at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, before Peter's confession, at the transfiguration, in Gethsemane, and on the cross. Only Luke records the parables of the persistent friend at midnight, the persistent widow, and the Pharisee and the tax collector praying in the temple. Prayer in Luke is the ordinary posture of those who wait on God.

themes.title: The Holy Spirit
themes.body: The Spirit is active from the first chapter: John is filled with the Spirit from the womb, Mary conceives by the Spirit's power, and Elizabeth, Zechariah, and Simeon speak by the Spirit. Jesus is anointed by the Spirit at his baptism and returns to Galilee in the Spirit's power. At the end he promises the disciples power from on high, which comes at Pentecost in Acts 2.

themes.title: Salvation today, and joy
themes.body: The word today carries weight in Luke: today a Savior is born (2:11), today the Scripture is fulfilled (4:21), today salvation has come to Zacchaeus's house (19:9), today the thief will be with Jesus in paradise (23:43). Salvation is present, not only future. And it brings joy: the angels announce good news of great joy, and heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents (15:7).

themes.title: Fulfillment and divine necessity
themes.body: Luke's first sentence speaks of things fulfilled among us, and the Greek word dei, it is necessary, marks the plan of God throughout: the boy must be in his Father's house (2:49), the Son of Man must suffer (9:22), and everything written must be fulfilled (24:44). History in Luke is not random; it is the working out of what God promised in the Scriptures.

keyChapters.why: The preface explains Luke's method, and the announcements to Zechariah and Mary, with Mary's song, set out the book's themes of reversal and fulfillment.
The birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, the shepherds, and Simeon's words about a light for the Gentiles anchor the good news in history and point to its reach.
Jesus' sermon at Nazareth from Isaiah 61 is his program statement for the whole ministry, and his rejection there foreshadows what follows.
The parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son show God's joy in finding the lost and expose the resentment of those who think they were never lost.
Zacchaeus's conversion and Jesus' statement that he came to seek and to save the lost lead into his entry into Jerusalem.
The empty tomb, the Emmaus road, and the ascension show the risen Jesus opening the Scriptures and sending his disciples to the nations.

text:
Luke's text is well attested and early. The oldest substantial witness is P75 (Papyrus Bodmer XIV-XV), a codex of Luke and John usually dated around AD 175 to 225, though some papyrologists place it later; it came to the Vatican Library in 2006 and 2007 and is now called the Hanna Papyrus. Its text is strikingly close to that of Codex Vaticanus, copied more than a century later. P4, fragments of Luke 1 to 6 in Paris found in the binding of a later codex of Philo, is also early; T. C. Skeat argued it came from the same codex as the Matthew fragments P64 and P67, though that is disputed. P45 (the Chester Beatty papyrus, third century) preserves parts of all four Gospels and Acts. The fourth-century codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, the fifth-century Alexandrinus and Washingtonianus, and early Latin, Syriac, and Coptic translations fill out the picture.

Luke also has a distinctive textual problem. Codex Bezae (fifth century) and the Old Latin carry a Western text of Luke and Acts, fuller in Acts and at several points shorter in Luke. Westcott and Hort (1881) judged some of Bezae's shorter readings in Luke 22 and 24 original and called them Western non-interpolations; most editors now keep the longer text. So English Bibles differ. The prayer from the cross, ‘Father, forgive them’ (23:34), is missing from P75, Vaticanus, and the first hand of Bezae, and modern Bibles print it with a note or in brackets. The angel and the sweat like drops of blood (22:43-44) are absent from P75 and Vaticanus but present in Sinaiticus and Bezae. The longer account of the Last Supper (22:19b-20) is missing only from Bezae and some Latin and Syriac witnesses. The Lord's Prayer in Luke (11:2-4) is shorter in the earliest manuscripts than the King James Version, which reflects later copyists filling it out from Matthew 6. The angels' song in 2:14 differs by one letter between ‘goodwill toward men’ and ‘people of his good pleasure’. In the story of the woman caught in adultery, one family of manuscripts places it after Luke 21:38 instead of in John.

The oldest evidence for Luke comes from Marcion of Sinope, who broke with the church at Rome around AD 144 and used a single Gospel, without an author's name, closely related to Luke but shorter: it lacked chapters 1 and 2 and began with Jesus coming down to Capernaum in the fifteenth year of Tiberius. It survives only through its opponents, chiefly Tertullian (Against Marcion, book 4) and Epiphanius (Panarion 42). Those writers, and Adolf von Harnack's reconstruction (1921), treat it as Marcion's cut-down Luke, edited to remove what tied Jesus to Israel's God. John Knox (Marcion and the New Testament, 1942) proposed that canonical Luke was instead expanded from an earlier gospel that Marcion also used, and Joseph Tyson (2006) developed a version of that view. Matthias Klinghardt (2015) and Markus Vinzent (2014) argued that Marcion's Gospel came first, and Jason BeDuhn (The First New Testament, 2013) that it was an older text Marcion adopted. Dieter Roth's critical reconstruction (The Text of Marcion's Gospel, 2015), now the standard, shows how much of that Gospel is uncertain; most scholars still conclude that Marcion edited Luke.
reception:
Luke was read as the Gospel of Paul's companion from the second century. Justin Martyr drew on its birth story, Marcion's use of it forced the church to defend it as one of four, and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.11.8) gave it the calf among the four living creatures of Revelation 4 because it begins with Zechariah the priest at the altar; Jerome, in the preface to his commentary on Matthew, kept the calf or ox for Luke, and the winged ox marks Luke on lecterns and in manuscripts such as the Book of Kells. Origen preached on it at Caesarea, and thirty-nine of his homilies survive in Jerome's Latin translation. Ambrose of Milan's Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke (about 387), ten books drawn from his sermons, is the fullest Latin patristic commentary on Luke. Cyril of Alexandria's 156 homilies on Luke survive mainly in a Syriac translation brought to England from the Egyptian desert in the 1840s. Bede wrote a commentary on it in eighth-century Northumbria, and Bonaventure and Thomas Aquinas (in his Catena Aurea) carried it through the Middle Ages.

Luke's hymns entered the church's daily prayer: the Benedictus at the morning office, the Magnificat at evening prayer, and the Nunc Dimittis at Compline, a pattern the Book of Common Prayer (1549) kept in Morning and Evening Prayer. The Ave Maria and the Angelus draw on Luke 1, and the Gloria in excelsis on Luke 2:14. The church year follows Luke through Advent and Christmas, the Annunciation on 25 March, the Visitation, and the Presentation on 2 February (Candlemas). From the sixth century (Theodore Lector, around 530) a legend held that Luke painted the Virgin, which made him the patron of painters and underlies Rogier van der Weyden's Saint Luke Drawing the Virgin (about 1435 to 1440). Luke's parables gave European art the Good Samaritan and Rembrandt's Return of the Prodigal Son (late 1660s), and his birth story gave music Bach's Magnificat (1723) and Christmas Oratorio (1734), Handel's Messiah (1742), and countless carols.

Modern criticism made Luke a theologian as well as a historian. Henry Cadbury studied its style and making (1920, 1927); Hans Conzelmann (1954) read it as a theology of salvation history written to cope with the delay of Christ's return; and the commentaries of I. Howard Marshall (1978), Joseph Fitzmyer (1981 and 1985), Luke Timothy Johnson (1991), Joel Green (1997), and François Bovon (2002 to 2013) set the modern standard. Liberation theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez made Luke's good news to the poor central to their reading, while feminist scholars have debated whether Luke honors women or confines them: Jane Schaberg, writing on Luke in The Women's Bible Commentary (1992), argued that it models silent, supporting women, and Turid Karlsen Seim (The Double Message, 1994) found in Luke-Acts both real prominence and real restraint. Jewish readers have asked how Luke's positive picture of Jewish piety in its first chapters fits its sharp words about Israel's leaders later; Amy-Jill Levine and Ben Witherington III wrote a commentary together (2018), a Jewish and a Christian scholar in conversation, that treats these questions and the book's use in Christian anti-Judaism openly.

furtherReading.author: N. T. Wright
furtherReading.title: Luke for Everyone
furtherReading.note: Short passages with a fresh translation and warm, historically informed reflection; an easy place for a newcomer to begin.

furtherReading.author: Michael Wilcock
furtherReading.title: The Message of Luke
furtherReading.note: A clear evangelical exposition that follows the shape of Luke's narrative and its Old Testament roots, written with preaching in view.

furtherReading.author: Joel B. Green
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of Luke
furtherReading.series: New International Commentary on the New Testament
furtherReading.note: Reads Luke as a unified narrative in its first-century social world; strong on the book's theology of salvation and its concern for the marginal.

furtherReading.author: Darrell L. Bock
furtherReading.title: Luke
furtherReading.series: Baker Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament
furtherReading.note: A thorough two-volume evangelical commentary (1994 and 1996), careful on the Greek, historical questions, and the views of other interpreters.

furtherReading.author: Luke Timothy Johnson
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of Luke
furtherReading.note: A Roman Catholic literary reading that attends to how Luke tells the story and to its prophetic pattern.

furtherReading.author: Amy-Jill Levine and Ben Witherington III
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of Luke
furtherReading.note: A Jewish and a Christian scholar comment together, showing where they agree and differ and how Luke has been used and misused.

furtherReading.author: Arthur A. Just Jr., editor
furtherReading.title: Luke
furtherReading.note: Selections from Origen, Ambrose, Cyril of Alexandria, Bede, and other early interpreters, arranged passage by passage.

furtherReading.author: Joseph A. Fitzmyer
furtherReading.title: The Gospel According to Luke
furtherReading.note: A landmark two-volume critical commentary (1981 and 1985) by a Jesuit scholar, with a long introduction to Luke's sources, theology, and Greek.

furtherReading.author: François Bovon
furtherReading.title: Luke
furtherReading.note: A three-volume historical-critical commentary (2002 to 2013) by a Swiss Protestant scholar, rich in the history of interpretation.

furtherReading.author: I. Howard Marshall
furtherReading.title: The Gospel of Luke
furtherReading.note: A detailed commentary on the Greek text, strong on Luke as historian and theologian.

furtherReading.author: Raymond E. Brown
furtherReading.title: The Birth of the Messiah
furtherReading.note: The standard study of the infancy narratives of Matthew and Luke, updated in 1993; indispensable for Luke 1 and 2.

furtherReading.author: Loveday Alexander
furtherReading.title: The Preface to Luke's Gospel
furtherReading.series: Society for New Testament Studies Monograph Series
furtherReading.note: Compares Luke 1:1-4 and Acts 1:1 with ancient prefaces and argues that Luke's closest models are Greek technical treatises.

furtherReading.author: Mark Goodacre
furtherReading.title: The Case Against Q
furtherReading.note: The fullest modern case for the Farrer hypothesis, that Luke used Mark and Matthew; read with a defense of the Two-Source view for balance.
